stories.the_lesson: Tax-collection data is one of the fastest real-time windows into how an economy is actually behaving — because it's tied directly to purchases as they happen, it often moves before slower, official growth statistics catch up.
stories.market_link: Strong consumption-tax data tends to support consumption and FMCG stocks and reinforces the case for the RBI to hold rather than cut rates.

stories.title: India's exporters brace for steeper US tariffs as the August 1 trade-deal deadline passes without an agreement
key_points: The **August 1 deadline** for a US-India interim trade deal passed with **no agreement reached**.
Reports say India-bound goods could face tariffs of **20–25%**, with President Trump earlier warning of rates up to **35%** for countries without a deal.
Talks are stuck because India won't open its politically sensitive **agriculture and dairy sectors**, while the US won't budge on India's steel, aluminium and auto tariff demands.
A US trade team is now expected in New Delhi only around **August 25**, pushing any resolution well past this month.
This follows a separate **February 2026** interim deal that had already cut US tariffs on Indian goods from 50% to 18% — leaving exporters facing a confusing, still-unsettled picture.
stories.background: The US and India have been negotiating a broader bilateral trade agreement for much of 2026, layered on top of an earlier interim deal reached in February that lowered tariffs on Indian goods. Trump has separately imposed a wave of country-by-country tariff deadlines this year — including the 35% Canada tariff and 10% global baseline that took effect this week — as leverage in trade negotiations worldwide. India's refusal to open agriculture and dairy to US imports, a politically explosive issue given the number of Indian farmers involved, has been the central sticking point in the broader talks.
stories.what_happened: Indian and US trade negotiators failed to finalize an interim agreement before President Trump's **August 1 deadline**, meaning Indian exporters now face the prospect of higher tariffs on goods sent to the US. Trump had previously said imports from India could be hit with rates of **20 to 25%** if no deal was reached, while his broader deadline framework threatens **tariffs as high as 35%** for countries without agreements. The talks remain deadlocked specifically over India's refusal to lower tariffs on **agricultural and dairy imports** from the US, while Washington has resisted India's demands for relief on **steel, aluminium and auto tariffs**. Adding to the uncertainty, a US trade delegation is now expected to visit New Delhi only around **August 25** to resume talks — meaning a resolution is unlikely this month or possibly next.
stories.why_it_matters: Export-heavy sectors — textiles, gems and jewellery, and pharmaceuticals among them — lose price competitiveness against rivals like Vietnam and Bangladesh if US tariffs stay elevated. For an economy that has been leaning on export growth, a prolonged standoff adds cost pressure right as India navigates other global shocks like the Gaza and Hormuz crises.
stories.ripple_effects: Expect exporters to lobby the government for relief measures or subsidies, added pressure on the rupee if trade flows weaken, and continued uncertainty for companies planning US-bound shipments. It also complicates India's broader trade diplomacy, coming as the country balances ties with the US against deepening trade ties elsewhere, including the reopened India-China border trade routes.
stories.why_now: The deadline itself fell on August 1, and talks visibly stalled going into it.
stories.watch_next: Whether the US Trade Representative's office confirms a specific new tariff rate for India, and what comes out of the delayed August 25 New Delhi talks.

key_terms.definition: A tax a country charges on goods imported from abroad — higher tariffs make foreign goods more expensive, which can protect domestic industries but also raise costs for consumers and exporters on the other side.

stories.the_lesson: Trade negotiations rarely fail over headline numbers — they usually stall on a handful of politically sensitive carve-outs (here, agriculture and dairy) that matter disproportionately more to domestic politics than their economic size suggests.
stories.market_link: India's export-oriented sectors (textiles, gems & jewellery, pharmaceuticals) and the rupee are directly exposed to how this resolves.

stories.title: India closes out its best-ever Commonwealth Games with 39 medals — and takes the baton as 2030 host
key_points: India finished the Glasgow 2026 Games with **39 medals**: **13 gold, 17 silver, 9 bronze** — its best-ever tally despite a curtailed sports program.
Boxing delivered India's best-ever CWG haul: **10 medals, including 7 golds**.
India's judo team won its **first-ever CWG judo golds**, taking its tally to four medals in the sport.
At the closing ceremony, India performed a **20-minute cultural showcase** led by Shankar Mahadevan and Manushi Chhillar as the Games flag was formally **handed to Ahmedabad**.
**Ahmedabad will host the 2030 Commonwealth Games** — India's first time hosting since Delhi in 2010.
stories.background: The 2026 Commonwealth Games ran in Glasgow from **July 23 to August 2**, a scaled-down edition of the event after several traditional host cities passed on bidding. India has steadily built up its Commonwealth Games strength in boxing, wrestling and weightlifting over the past two decades, and this edition marked a breakthrough in judo, a sport where India had never previously won gold at the Games. Ahmedabad's selection as 2030 host — confirmed in the run-up to this year's Games — makes it India's first Commonwealth Games since Delhi 2010, a Games remembered as much for infrastructure and corruption controversies as for sport.
stories.what_happened: The Glasgow 2026 Commonwealth Games concluded on **Sunday, August 2**, with a closing ceremony at the Hydro arena. India ended the Games with **39 medals** — 13 gold, 17 silver and 9 bronze — its best tally at a Commonwealth Games to date, even with a smaller sports program than previous editions. **Boxing** was the standout, delivering a best-ever **10 medals including 7 golds**, headlined by wins from **Preeti Pawar** and **Arundhati Choudhary**. India's **judo** team won its first-ever CWG golds through **Asmita Dey** and **Harsh Singh**, building a four-medal tally in a sport where the country had no prior history of Commonwealth success. At the closing ceremony, Indian performers **Shankar Mahadevan** and **Manushi Chhillar** led a 20-minute cultural showcase before the Commonwealth Games flag was formally handed over to representatives of **Ahmedabad**, confirmed as host of the **2030 Games**.
stories.why_it_matters: A best-ever medal count, and a breakthrough in a sport (judo) where India had no prior Commonwealth pedigree, signals real depth building beyond India's traditional strongholds of wrestling and shooting. Hosting the 2030 Games is also a major statement of intent — the first time India has hosted a global multi-sport event since the mixed legacy of Delhi 2010.
stories.ripple_effects: Expect a funding and attention boost for boxing and judo heading into the next Olympic cycle, and the start of a long infrastructure and organizational build-up in Ahmedabad ahead of 2030. India's Cabinet has already cleared a ₹36,441 crore overhaul of the Khelo India sports scheme, partly a response to this year's showing.
stories.why_now: The Games' closing ceremony and final medal count happened today, August 2.
stories.watch_next: Early details on Ahmedabad's 2030 Games infrastructure and budget plans, and whether India's boxing/judo funding increases follow through in the next Union Budget.
stories.the_lesson: Sporting success in new disciplines (like India's judo breakthrough here) usually reflects years of quiet grassroots investment before it shows up on a medal table — a single Games rarely creates a new strength, it reveals one that was already being built.

stories.title: India and China reopen Himalayan border trade routes after a six-year freeze
key_points: Barter trade resumed through **three Himalayan passes** — Shipki La, Nathu La and Lipulekh — on **August 1**
The routes had been shut for **six years**, since 2019, over Covid and heightened border tensions
**16 local traders** carried out the first expedition through Shipki La in Himachal Pradesh's Kinnaur district
Traders can carry **72 types of goods** into Tibet and bring back **30 types**, returning within **72 hours**
Himachal's Revenue Minister **Jagat Singh Negi** flagged off the traders with a traditional ceremony
stories.background: Shipki La, Nathu La and Lipulekh are ancient Himalayan trade passes connecting Indian border communities with Tibet for centuries, long before the modern India-China border existed. Local traders would carry goods across on a **barter system** — no cash changes hands, goods are simply exchanged for goods — sustaining livelihoods in remote mountain districts. Border trade through these passes was suspended in **2019**, first over pandemic restrictions and then because of the sharp deterioration in India-China relations after their **2020 military clash in Ladakh**, which froze most cross-border cooperation for years.
stories.what_happened: On **August 1**, India and China resumed border trade through all three passes for the first time in six years. In Himachal Pradesh's Kinnaur district, **16 local traders** set off on the first expedition through **Shipki La** towards Shipki village in Tibet, carrying goods on horseback after a ceremonial send-off by Revenue and Horticulture Minister **Jagat Singh Negi**, who presented the traders with traditional ceremonial scarves. Under the trade rules, Indian traders can carry **72 types of items** across, while goods coming back from the Tibetan side are limited to **30 types**; traders must complete their business and return within **72 hours**. Similar resumptions took place at Nathu La in Sikkim and Lipulekh in Uttarakhand.
stories.why_it_matters: This is a small but symbolically significant sign that India-China relations are thawing after years of military tension along their disputed Himalayan border. Reopening trade routes shut for six years signals both sides are willing to restore at least limited normal ties, even as the underlying border disputes remain unresolved.
stories.ripple_effects: For remote Himalayan border communities in Kinnaur, Sikkim and Uttarakhand, the reopening restores a traditional source of income and revives cultural and tourism links with Tibet. More broadly, it could be an early, low-risk step toward a wider thaw — but any fresh border incident could just as easily freeze it again.
stories.why_now: The resumption follows a broader recent effort by India and China to ease tensions, including resumed direct flights and diplomatic visits, after years of near-total freeze following the 2020 Ladakh clash.
stories.watch_next: Watch for whether India and China take further confidence-building steps, such as expanding trade volumes or resuming other suspended cooperation, in the coming months.

key_terms.definition: An exchange of goods for goods without money changing hands — the traditional system used at these Himalayan border posts.

stories.the_lesson: Even amid unresolved geopolitical disputes, countries often keep small, symbolic channels of cooperation — like local border trade — open as a way to signal goodwill without having to resolve the bigger disagreements first.

stories.title: RBI set to hold interest rates steady for a sixth straight meeting even as India's economy runs hotter than expected
key_points: The RBI's rate-setting committee meets **August 3–5**, with the decision due **August 5 at 10am IST**
**68 of 72 economists** polled by Reuters expect the RBI to hold the repo rate at **5.25%**
**SBI Research** estimates India's economy could have grown **more than 7%** in the April–June quarter
Retail inflation rose to **4.38%** in June, back above the RBI's 4% target
The hold reflects the RBI balancing **strong growth** against **inflation, a weaker rupee, and global uncertainty**
stories.background: The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) sets the **repo rate** — the interest rate at which it lends to commercial banks — roughly every two months through its Monetary Policy Committee (MPC). That rate ripples through the economy: it shapes what banks charge on home loans and business credit, and how much they pay savers on fixed deposits. India's central bank has held rates unchanged at 5.25% for months, a level it judges low enough to support growth without overheating prices. Governor **Sanjay Malhotra** has repeatedly said the RBI wants inflation durably near its 4% target before cutting further.
stories.what_happened: India's MPC meets from **August 3 to 5**, with the decision due August 5 at 10am IST. The overwhelming consensus among economists — 68 of 72 surveyed by Reuters — is that the RBI will hold the repo rate at **5.25%**, even though early estimates from SBI Research suggest the economy may have grown faster than **7%** in the April–June quarter (Q1 of fiscal year 2026–27), beating expectations. The reason for caution: retail inflation climbed back to **4.38%** in June, above the RBI's 4% target, and the central bank is also watching a wobblier rupee and global trade uncertainty, including fresh US tariffs. Only four of the surveyed economists expect a hike, and none expect a cut.
stories.why_it_matters: The repo rate decision touches nearly every Indian household and business — it shapes home loan EMIs, business borrowing costs and fixed deposit returns. A hold means no immediate relief on loan payments, but also no rate hike that would make borrowing costlier, at a moment when growth is strong but so is inflation.
stories.ripple_effects: A steady rate keeps India's growth story attractive to investors even as the US and other economies wrestle with slower growth, which could keep foreign money flowing into Indian markets. But if inflation keeps climbing, the RBI may have less room to cut rates later in the year even if growth slows.
stories.why_now: The MPC meets on a fixed roughly bimonthly cycle, and this meeting is the first major checkpoint after June's inflation uptick and the first growth estimates for the new fiscal year.
stories.watch_next: Watch the RBI's official decision and Governor Malhotra's press conference on August 5 for the exact rate call and updated inflation and growth forecasts.

key_terms.definition: The interest rate at which the RBI lends money to commercial banks — a lower rate makes borrowing cheaper across the economy, a higher rate makes it more expensive.

stories.the_lesson: A central bank doesn't just react to growth or inflation alone — it weighs both together, and strong growth alone isn't enough to trigger a rate cut if inflation is still running above target.
stories.market_link: A hold is broadly priced in by Indian bond and equity markets; a surprise hike could pressure rate-sensitive sectors like banking, auto and real estate stocks, while a surprise cut would likely boost them.

stories.title: India's boxing golden run continues at the Commonwealth Games: Arundhati Choudhary wins gold, Lovlina Borgohain takes silver
key_points: **Arundhati Choudhary** beat Olympic and World Championships bronze medallist Chantelle Reid **5-0** to win women's 70kg gold.
It's India's **fifth boxing gold** of the Glasgow 2026 Games, extending the country's best-ever CWG boxing showing.
**Lovlina Borgohain** lost a close **4-1 split decision** to Australia's Emma-Sue Greentree in the women's 75kg final, settling for silver.
Lovlina's silver completes a **full medal set** — she now has medals from the Olympics, Worlds, Asian Games, and Commonwealth Games.
All **10 Indian boxers** who entered the finals this Games have now medalled, a historic sweep for the contingent.
stories.background: India sent an unusually large and talented boxing squad to the Glasgow 2026 Commonwealth Games, and **all 10 boxers who reached the finals won at least a medal** — the best Commonwealth Games boxing performance in the country's history. Lovlina Borgohain, a Tokyo Olympic bronze medallist, is one of India's most decorated boxers, while 70kg gold medallist Arundhati Choudhary has been rising through the ranks against senior international opposition. Boxing has become one of India's most reliable medal sports at multi-discipline events, alongside wrestling and shooting.
stories.what_happened: On the boxing finals day at Glasgow 2026, **Arundhati Choudhary defeated England's Chantelle Reid — an Olympic and World Championships bronze medallist — by a unanimous 5-0 verdict** to win the women's 70kg gold medal, taking India's tally to **five golds** in the ring. In the marquee women's 75kg final, **Lovlina Borgohain lost a tight 4-1 split decision to Australia's Emma-Sue Greentree**, who did enough across the bout to convince a majority of judges despite Lovlina's composed, technical performance. The silver adds to Lovlina's collection, giving her podium finishes at the Olympics, World Championships, Asian Games, and now the Commonwealth Games. Across the Games, **all 10 Indian boxers who reached finals medalled**, a clean sweep that officials are calling the country's best-ever Commonwealth Games boxing campaign.
stories.why_it_matters: This cements boxing as a genuine Indian medal powerhouse alongside wrestling and shooting, with depth beyond individual stars — 10 finalists all medalling is a squad-wide achievement, not a one-off. It also builds momentum and funding case for Indian boxing heading toward the next Olympic cycle.
stories.ripple_effects: Expect increased sports-ministry funding attention and sponsorship interest in boxing following this campaign, echoed by the Cabinet's recent ₹36,441 crore Khelo India scheme expansion aimed at building on exactly this kind of results. Young boxers, especially women, are likely to see a bump in grassroots interest off the back of this coverage.
stories.why_now: The Glasgow 2026 boxing finals concluded today, the culmination of India's ring campaign at these Games.
stories.watch_next: India's overall medal tally and finishing position on the Commonwealth Games table as the event wraps up, and whether this boxing generation carries form into the 2028 Olympic qualification cycle.

key_terms.definition: A boxing judging result where the judges don't agree unanimously — here, 4 of 5 judges scored the bout for Greentree, one for Lovlina.

stories.the_lesson: A country's strength in a sport is best measured not by one star medallist but by how deep the podium finishes go — India's 10-for-10 boxing final record shows a genuine talent pipeline, not a fluke.

stories.title: India's judo team wins a fourth Commonwealth Games medal as Unnati Sharma battles to bronze in Glasgow
key_points: Unnati Sharma wins **bronze in the women's -63kg** category, India's **fourth judo medal** of the 2026 Games.
She opened with an **ippon win** over Eswatini's Lamulela Magagula, then edged New Zealand's Qona Christie in the quarter-finals.
A semi-final loss to eventual silver medallist **Saya Middleton** of Australia sent her into the bronze playoff.
She sealed bronze with an **ippon in just 1:07 minutes** over South Africa's Skye Knoester.
Teammates **Karanjit Singh Maan** and **Harsh Tokas** both fell just short of the podium in their own weight categories today.
stories.background: Judo has historically been a minor medal source for India at the Commonwealth Games, with the contingent traditionally built around athletics, wrestling and boxing. That changed at Glasgow 2026: judokas **Asmita Dey and Harsh Singh** had already won India's first-ever Commonwealth Games judo golds earlier in the Games. Unnati Sharma, competing in the women's -63kg category, was part of a young judo squad hoping to build on that breakthrough. In judo scoring, a full point (ippon) wins a bout outright, while lesser scores (waza-ari) can add up — meaning matches can turn in seconds.
stories.what_happened: On day 9 of the Glasgow 2026 Commonwealth Games, Unnati Sharma won bronze in the women's -63kg judo category, taking India's judo medal tally at these Games to four. She began with an ippon victory over Eswatini's Lamulela Magagula in the round of 16, then narrowly beat New Zealand's Qona Christie by waza-ari in the quarter-finals to reach the last four. In the semi-final she lost by ippon to Australia's Saya Middleton, who went on to win silver, dropping Sharma into the bronze-medal playoff. She won that decisively, defeating South Africa's Skye Knoester by ippon in just **one minute and seven seconds**. Two teammates, Karanjit Singh Maan (men's -90kg) and Harsh Tokas (men's -81kg), reached their own bronze-medal contests today but both lost, ending their medal hopes.
stories.why_it_matters: A fourth judo medal in a single Games is a genuine breakthrough for a sport India has rarely medalled in at this level, hinting at a talent pipeline that could carry into future Olympic cycles. It also adds to what is shaping up as one of India's best-ever overall Commonwealth Games showings, alongside historic hauls in boxing and athletics.
stories.ripple_effects: A strong multi-sport showing typically feeds back into domestic sports funding — disciplines that medal at events like this tend to see increased grants and athlete support in the following years. It also raises the profile of judo as an option for young Indian athletes choosing which sport to pursue competitively.
stories.why_now: Day 9 was a heavy medal day across combat and individual sports for India at Glasgow 2026, with judo, boxing and athletics finals all scheduled the same day.
stories.watch_next: Watch India's remaining judo entries, including Inunganbi Takhellambam, for whether the tally climbs further before the competition concludes.

key_terms.definition: The highest score in judo — a clean, decisive throw or hold that ends the match immediately, similar to a knockout in boxing.
A judo score worth less than an ippon; two waza-ari scores in one bout equal an ippon and end the match.

stories.the_lesson: A country's medal strength in a sport often traces back to a single breakthrough generation — once a few athletes prove a discipline is winnable, it tends to attract more investment and more competitors chasing the same success.

stories.title: India opens a ₹4,000 crore credit line for Bhutan's energy projects as ties deepen
key_points: India signed a **₹4,000 crore concessional Line of Credit** with Bhutan, dedicated to **energy projects**.
The deal was signed during Foreign Secretary **Vikram Misri's** two-day visit to Thimphu.
The two countries also approved **12 new development projects** worth ₹332 crore.
It's **separate from** India's existing **₹10,000 crore** support package for Bhutan's current Five-Year Plan (2024-2029).
The credit line carries **below-market interest rates**, making it cheaper for Bhutan to borrow than through commercial lenders.
stories.background: Bhutan is one of India's closest strategic partners, sandwiched between India and China in the Himalayas, and India has long been its largest aid donor, trading partner, and hydropower investor. India has funded major hydropower plants in Bhutan for decades, buying the electricity back to help meet its own power needs while giving landlocked Bhutan a crucial source of export revenue. Delhi treats close ties with Thimphu as strategically important given Bhutan's position along a stretch of the disputed India-China border, including near the sensitive **Doklam plateau**, where Indian and Chinese troops faced off in 2017.
stories.what_happened: India's Foreign Secretary **Vikram Misri** concluded a two-day visit to Bhutan's capital, Thimphu, during which the two countries signed a **₹4,000 crore** concessional Line of Credit agreement between India's Export-Import Bank and Bhutan's finance ministry, earmarked for energy projects. Misri and his Bhutanese counterpart, **Dasho Pema Lektup Dorji**, co-chaired the fifth round of India-Bhutan Development Cooperation Talks, covering Bhutan's ongoing 13th Five-Year Plan. The two sides also approved **12 new projects** worth a combined ₹332 crore. Officials described the credit line as separate from and additional to India's existing ₹10,000 crore support package for Bhutan's current five-year plan, which runs from 2024 to 2029.
stories.why_it_matters: Bhutan sits in a strategically sensitive spot between India and China, and India's economic support helps keep Thimphu firmly in Delhi's orbit rather than drifting toward closer ties with Beijing, which has been pushing its own border and diplomatic overtures to Bhutan in recent years.
stories.ripple_effects: For Bhutan, cheap financing lowers the cost of building out hydropower and other energy infrastructure it can export back to India. For India, deeper energy ties secure a nearby, reliable source of clean hydropower and reinforce its influence in a country China would also like closer ties with.
stories.why_now: The credit line was formalized during a scheduled round of bilateral development talks, but it also comes as China has been separately pursuing direct border talks and outreach with Bhutan, adding urgency to India's efforts to stay Thimphu's primary partner.
stories.watch_next: Which specific energy projects in Bhutan draw on the new credit line first, and whether China makes any competing overtures to Thimphu in response.

key_terms.definition: A loan facility offered at below-market interest rates or with longer repayment terms, usually from one government to another to fund specific projects.

stories.the_lesson: Small, steady economic commitments — a credit line here, a set of joint projects there — are often how larger geopolitical influence is actually built and maintained, rather than through single dramatic gestures.

stories.title: India's Cabinet approves ₹84,084 crore 'Samudra Manthan' scheme to hunt for offshore oil and gas
key_points: The Cabinet approved **'Samudra Manthan'**, a **₹84,084 crore** national offshore exploration scheme running through **FY2030-31**.
It funds **60 deepwater exploration wells** (₹43,200 crore) and modern **offshore seismic surveys** (₹28,534 crore) to map the seabed for oil and gas.
The government will cover up to **50% of drilling costs per well** (capped at ₹675 crore) to de-risk exploration for companies.
The scheme targets adding over **600 million tonnes of oil equivalent** to India's proven reserves.
Officials say the extra output could cut India's crude **import bill by nearly ₹1 lakh crore a year**.
stories.background: India imports roughly **85% of the crude oil** it consumes, making it highly exposed to global oil-price swings and supply shocks — a vulnerability that's been on display this year as the US-Iran conflict pushed oil prices higher. Offshore exploration in Indian waters has lagged partly because deepwater drilling is expensive and risky, discouraging private companies from bidding aggressively. The government has previously tried to boost domestic output through auction reforms like the Open Acreage Licensing Policy, with mixed results. Samudra Manthan is the government's biggest single push yet to directly subsidize the riskiest, most capital-intensive part of that search: deepwater and ultra-deepwater drilling.
stories.what_happened: The Union Cabinet, chaired by Prime Minister **Narendra Modi**, approved the 'Samudra Manthan' (Ocean Churning) National Offshore Exploration Scheme on Friday, with a total outlay of **₹84,084 crore** to be spent through FY2030-31. The scheme has four components: **₹28,534 crore** for modern offshore seismic surveys to map likely reserves, **₹43,200 crore** to drill **60 deepwater exploration wells** — with the government covering up to 50% of each well's cost or ₹675 crore, whichever is lower — **₹10,000 crore** for shared offshore infrastructure hubs to help commercialize discoveries, and further funding to build a domestic offshore technology and manufacturing base under 'Make in India.' The government estimates the scheme could add more than **600 million tonnes of oil equivalent** to India's hydrocarbon reserves and cut annual crude oil imports by close to **₹1 lakh crore**.
stories.why_it_matters: India's oil import bill is one of the biggest drags on its trade balance and a direct channel through which global oil-price shocks — like this year's Iran conflict — hit Indian inflation and the rupee. Meaningfully raising domestic output would reduce that exposure and free up foreign exchange for other uses.
stories.ripple_effects: If exploration succeeds, it benefits state oil majors like ONGC and private players such as Reliance and Vedanta who bid for offshore blocks, and supports India's oil-services and shipbuilding sectors under the 'Make in India' push. A lower import bill also eases pressure on the rupee and the current account deficit over time. But deepwater drilling typically takes years to translate into actual production, so any impact on imports is a medium-to-long-term story, not immediate.
stories.why_now: The announcement lands the same week global oil prices touched a one-month high on US-Iran conflict fears, underscoring why India is trying to reduce its reliance on imported crude.
stories.watch_next: The first exploration licensing round under the new scheme, and how many companies bid for the deepwater blocks on offer.

key_terms.definition: Drilling for oil and gas in ocean waters far deeper than shallow coastal wells, which is more technically difficult and expensive but can access larger reserves.
A standard unit used to compare different fuels — like oil, gas, and coal — by converting them to the energy value of an equivalent amount of crude oil.

stories.the_lesson: Governments often subsidize the riskiest, most capital-intensive stage of an industry — here, deepwater drilling — because private companies won't take that risk alone even when the long-term payoff (energy security) benefits the whole country.
stories.market_link: A credible path to higher domestic oil and gas output is a long-term positive for the rupee and for stocks like ONGC, Oil India, and Reliance's upstream business, though any production impact is years away.

stories.title: Modi inaugurates a new international airport and semiconductor plant in a ₹18,000 crore Andhra Pradesh push
key_points: Modi inaugurated projects worth nearly **₹18,000 crore ($2.1 billion)** in Andhra Pradesh.
The centerpiece: the new **Alluri Sitarama Raju International Airport** at Bhogapuram, built for **6 million passengers a year**.
He laid the foundation for a **₹460 crore semiconductor plant** with South Korea's APACT.
Also included: over **₹4,370 crore** in transmission infrastructure for wind and solar energy zones.
AP's coalition government — a key national NDA ally — hosted the visit.
stories.background: Andhra Pradesh's government, led by Chief Minister **N. Chandrababu Naidu**'s Telugu Desam Party in coalition with **Pawan Kalyan**'s Jana Sena, is a significant ally of the BJP-led coalition at the national level, and big central infrastructure investment there reflects that political relationship. The new airport is named after **Alluri Sitarama Raju**, a tribal freedom fighter who led an armed uprising against British colonial rule in the 1920s. The semiconductor project connects to India's broader 'Make in India' push to build domestic chip-manufacturing capacity, part of a global race — especially amid US-China tech tensions — to reduce reliance on the small handful of countries, mainly Taiwan, that dominate advanced chip production today.
stories.what_happened: Prime Minister Narendra Modi visited Andhra Pradesh on **Saturday, August 1**, and inaugurated or laid foundation stones for projects worth close to **₹18,000 crore (about $2.1 billion)**. The headline project is the new **Alluri Sitarama Raju International Airport** at Bhogapuram in Vizianagaram district, built as a public-private partnership at a cost of over **₹5,640 crore**, designed to handle **6 million passengers a year**, roughly 45 km from Visakhapatnam. Modi also laid the foundation stone for a **₹460 crore semiconductor project** in Visakhapatnam, being built by ASIP Technologies with South Korea's **APACT**. Other projects included transmission infrastructure for the Kurnool Wind and Solar Energy Zone worth about ₹3,550 crore, and a POWERGRID transmission scheme serving 2,500 MW of solar capacity in Ananthapuram and 1,000 MW in Kurnool, worth over ₹820 crore. AP Chief Minister **N. Chandrababu Naidu** and Deputy CM **Pawan Kalyan** attended alongside Modi.
stories.why_it_matters: The semiconductor plant is a small but symbolically important step in India's push to build domestic chip-making capacity, an industry currently dominated by a handful of countries. The airport and renewable-energy transmission investment mark a significant infrastructure bet on Andhra Pradesh, a state whose ruling coalition is a key partner in the national government.
stories.ripple_effects: A new international airport can accelerate trade, tourism and investment into coastal Andhra Pradesh, while the renewable-energy transmission lines help the state actually deliver the solar and wind power it has been building capacity for. Continued high-value central investment in AP also reinforces the political relationship between Naidu's coalition and the national government ahead of future election cycles.
stories.why_now: The visit and inaugurations were scheduled for today, timed as a showcase of the state government's infrastructure delivery record.
stories.watch_next: Watch for the semiconductor plant's construction timeline and the airport's first scheduled international flights.

key_terms.definition: An infrastructure project jointly funded and operated by a government body and a private company, sharing costs and risk.

stories.the_lesson: Big infrastructure inaugurations often double as political signals — the choice of state, timing, and attending officials can say as much about coalition politics as the ribbon-cutting itself.
stories.market_link: The semiconductor and renewable-energy transmission investments touch India's chip-manufacturing and clean-energy infrastructure themes that some listed industrial and power-transmission stocks track.

stories.title: Joe Root says new coach Stephen Fleming was a 'big reason' he agreed to take England's Test captaincy back
key_points: **Joe Root** is back as England's **Test captain**, four years after stepping down from the role.
New head coach **Stephen Fleming** was, in Root's own words, a **'big reason'** he wanted the job again.
The pair succeed **Brendon McCullum and Ben Stokes**, who stepped down as coach and captain respectively.
Root called himself **'very excited'** by how Fleming sees the game and where England needs to get to.
Root's first assignment is a **three-Test home series against Pakistan**.
stories.background: Joe Root is England's all-time leading Test run-scorer and previously captained the side for a record 64 matches between 2017 and 2022, before stepping down under pressure after a difficult run of results. Brendon McCullum and Ben Stokes then took England's Test side in a famously attacking direction, but both have now moved on from their respective coaching and captaincy roles, prompting the ECB to turn back to Root and bring in New Zealand great **Stephen Fleming** — previously head coach of IPL side Chennai Super Kings — as the new Test head coach.
stories.what_happened: Speaking after the ECB confirmed the new coaching and captaincy setup, **Joe Root** said that **Stephen Fleming's** appointment as England's Test head coach was a **'big reason'** he agreed to return as captain. Root said: **'We've spoken briefly and if I'm being brutally honest he was a big reason why I wanted to do it. I'm very excited by the way he sees the game, where he sees us sit as a team and the work we have to do to get to where we want to get to.'** The 35-year-old Root returns to the captaincy for the first time since his 2022 resignation, taking over from Ben Stokes, while Fleming replaces Brendon McCullum as head coach. Root's first assignment in the role will be a **three-Test home series against Pakistan starting August 19**, with Fleming's first assignment continuing into England's winter tour of South Africa.
stories.why_it_matters: Root's comments show the new captain-coach relationship is being built around a shared vision from day one, rather than Root simply being handed the job by default — that matters for how quickly a new leadership pairing can get a dressing room aligned.
stories.ripple_effects: England's Test team now heads into a home series against Pakistan, followed by a winter tour of South Africa, under an entirely new leadership axis — how quickly Root and Fleming's partnership clicks will shape selection calls and tactics for the rest of the cycle.
stories.why_now: Root's comments came the day after the ECB's formal announcement of the new roles, as he spoke publicly for the first time about why he chose to return to the captaincy.
stories.watch_next: How Root's captaincy and Fleming's coaching approach show up in team selection and tactics when the Pakistan series begins on August 19.
stories.the_lesson: Leadership changes in team sport often hinge less on the job title and more on whether the people involved trust each other's vision — Root's comments underline that the coach-captain relationship, not just ability, drives whether a comeback works.

stories.title: Jasprit Bumrah ruled out of India's upcoming Test series in Sri Lanka with a knee injury
key_points: India's premier fast bowler **Jasprit Bumrah** will miss the **two-Test series in Sri Lanka**, starting **August 15** in Galle.
The injury is **left knee discomfort** that Bumrah has been managing since the **T20 World Cup** earlier this year.
He first aggravated it while **fielding against England** in an ODI in Cardiff.
BCCI's medical team has advised **against rushing him back** before he's fully recovered.
**Auqib Nabi**, a Jammu & Kashmir seam-bowling all-rounder, is the **front-runner** to replace him in the squad.
stories.background: Jasprit Bumrah is widely regarded as the best fast bowler in world cricket and has carried a heavy fast-bowling workload for India across formats for years, including through this year's T20 World Cup. India's team management has been managing his workload carefully given a history of back and now knee issues, resting him from some matches to keep him available for the biggest series.
stories.what_happened: India's team management confirmed that **Jasprit Bumrah** will not be available for the upcoming **two-match Test series in Sri Lanka**, with the first Test starting in **Galle on August 15** and the second in **Colombo from August 23**. Bumrah has been nursing discomfort in his **left knee** since the T20 World Cup earlier this year, and re-aggravated the issue while fielding during a recent **ODI against England in Cardiff**. The BCCI's medical staff have advised that he needs more time to fully recover rather than risk returning early. **Auqib Nabi**, a seam-bowling all-rounder from Jammu & Kashmir, has emerged as the front-runner to be added to the squad as his replacement.
stories.why_it_matters: Bumrah is India's most important bowling weapon in Test cricket, especially overseas, where his pace and reverse-swing skills are frequently the difference-maker. Losing him for a series in conditions that can otherwise favor spin puts more pressure on India's other seamers and its spin attack to take 20 wickets without him.
stories.ripple_effects: India's team balance and bowling plans for the Sri Lanka series will likely shift toward more spin-friendly selections. It also keeps the spotlight on India's fast-bowling depth heading into a packed international calendar, and raises questions about workload management for its other frontline quicks.
stories.why_now: The news broke on August 2, less than two weeks before the first Test, giving India's selectors a narrow window to finalize a replacement squad.
stories.watch_next: Whether Auqib Nabi or another bowler is formally added to the Test squad, and any update on Bumrah's recovery timeline ahead of India's next assignments.
stories.the_lesson: Even the best individual player in a sport is a walking injury risk for the team that depends on them — squad depth, not just star power, decides how a team copes when its best player is unavailable.

stories.title: Sri Lanka Women seal a rare series win over Pakistan, snapping a 12-year drought
key_points: Sri Lanka won by **6 wickets** to seal the T20I series **2-0** with a match to spare
It's Sri Lanka's first bilateral T20I series win over Pakistan in **12 years**
**Harshitha Samarawickrama** hit an unbeaten 37 to guide the chase and was named player of the series
Pakistan's **Shawaal Zulfiqar** scored a maiden WT20I half-century, but it wasn't enough
Sri Lanka chased down Pakistan's **175/5** with balls to spare
stories.background: Sri Lanka Women and Pakistan Women don't play each other often in bilateral series, and Pakistan has historically had the upper hand — Sri Lanka hadn't beaten Pakistan in a bilateral **T20I series in 12 years**. This series, played in **Dambulla**, was a chance for Sri Lanka to end that streak against a Pakistan side searching for form of its own.
stories.what_happened: Sri Lanka Women beat Pakistan Women by **6 wickets** in the second T20I at the Rangiri Dambulla International Stadium, chasing down Pakistan's total of **175/5** with balls to spare, to win the two-match series **2-0**. **Harshitha Samarawickrama** finished unbeaten on 37 off 22 balls to see her team home, and was named player of the series after scoring 173 runs across the two matches, including an unbeaten century in the first game. For Pakistan, **Shawaal Zulfiqar** top-scored with a maiden WT20I half-century, but it wasn't enough to prevent the loss. The win ends a **12-year wait** for Sri Lanka to beat Pakistan in a bilateral T20I series.
stories.why_it_matters: It's a rare, meaningful marker of Sri Lanka Women's cricket rebuilding competitiveness against a traditionally stronger opponent, and a breakout series for Samarawickrama.
stories.ripple_effects: A confidence-boosting series win like this can help Sri Lanka Women's team building and player development heading into future white-ball assignments, while Pakistan will face scrutiny over their batting depth after failing to defend a competitive total twice.
stories.why_now: The series concluded today with the second and final T20I, sealing the result with a match still to play.
stories.watch_next: Watch how Samarawickrama's form carries into Sri Lanka's next assignments, and whether Pakistan makes squad changes in response to the series loss.
stories.the_lesson: In cricket, ending a long losing streak against a specific opponent often comes down to one or two individual players finally delivering consistently across a series, not just a single big performance.

stories.title: Jofra Archer's 4-9 sinks London Spirit at Lord's as Adil Rashid becomes The Hundred's all-time leading wicket-taker
key_points: Jofra Archer took **4 for 9** to bowl out London Spirit for 105 at Lord's, winning the Meerkat Match Hero award.
Southern Brave chased down the target, winning by **5 wickets with 3 balls to spare**.
Adil Rashid's **2 for 17** made him The Hundred men's competition's **all-time leading wicket-taker**, passing Tymal Mills.
Marcus Stoinis took 3 for 17 and now leads the tournament's wicket charts with **9 wickets in 4 matches**.
The result keeps Southern Brave alive for the Eliminator, while London Spirit's playoff hopes take a big hit.
stories.background: The Hundred is England's 100-ball franchise cricket tournament, now in its sixth season, running through August with a finals day on August 16 at Lord's. Southern Brave and London Spirit were both fighting for a place in the knockout stages, making this match — the 16th of the men's competition — a genuine four-points swing for the table.
stories.what_happened: At Lord's on August 1, London Spirit were bowled out for **105**, with Jonny Bairstow's 56 the only notable resistance, after Jofra Archer ripped through the middle order with figures of **4 for 9**. Marcus Stoinis chipped in with 3 for 17, extending his tournament-leading tally to **9 wickets in 4 matches**. Chasing 106, Southern Brave got home with **5 wickets and 3 balls in hand**, sealing a 5-wicket win. Adil Rashid, who took 2 for 17 in the match, became the **all-time leading wicket-taker in Hundred men's competition history**, overtaking previous record-holder Tymal Mills. Archer was named the match's Meerkat Match Hero for his bowling.
stories.why_it_matters: The win keeps Southern Brave firmly in the hunt for the Eliminator stage, while London Spirit's already difficult path to the knockouts gets tougher with the tournament's group phase winding down. Rashid's record also cements his status as one of the format's most consistently effective bowlers across multiple Hundred seasons.
stories.ripple_effects: The result reshuffles The Hundred men's points table with the group stage nearing its end, sharpening the race for the four playoff spots ahead of finals day on August 16 at Lord's. Strong recent form from Archer and Rashid also feeds into broader conversations about England's white-ball bowling options.
stories.why_now: This was a live group-stage match played today with direct table implications, and Rashid's record was set in the same match, making both storylines immediately current.
stories.watch_next: How the group table shakes out over the tournament's final matches before qualification for finals day on August 16.

key_terms.definition: The Hundred's official player-of-the-match award, sponsored by Compare the Market's Meerkat brand.

stories.the_lesson: In short-format cricket, a single devastating bowling spell — not just the final scoreline — is often what actually decides a tight match, which is why bowlers' figures matter as much as the result.

stories.title: Mumbai Indians shut the door on Hardik Pandya trade talks with CSK, as the saga stalls
key_points: **Mumbai Indians** have reportedly pulled back from active negotiations with **Chennai Super Kings (CSK)** over a Hardik Pandya trade, with no deal currently being pursued.
The sticking point had been MI's demand for **both Shivam Dube and young opener Ayush Mhatre** in exchange for their captain — CSK were unwilling to part with Mhatre.
MI's official line: they have **denied** reports that Pandya is being actively shopped, even as talks with multiple franchises had been ongoing.
**Delhi Capitals, Kolkata Knight Riders and Rajasthan Royals** had all separately been reported as interested parties before this pullback.
As things stand, **no trade has been completed** and Pandya's franchise future for the next season remains unresolved.
stories.background: **Hardik Pandya**, Mumbai Indians' captain and one of Indian cricket's premier all-rounders, has been at the center of an escalating trade saga this off-season, with multiple IPL franchises reportedly circling. CSK had proposed swapping all-rounder **Shivam Dube** for Pandya, while MI countered by asking for Dube plus rising opener **Ayush Mhatre** — a demand CSK were unwilling to meet given Mhatre's rising value. Delhi Capitals had separately floated a package built around Axar Patel and Prithvi Shaw (or Sameer Rizvi), while Kolkata Knight Riders and Rajasthan Royals had also made informal contact with MI. None of these discussions had been officially confirmed by any franchise before this latest development.
stories.what_happened: **Mumbai Indians** have reportedly stepped back from active trade discussions with **Chennai Super Kings** over their captain **Hardik Pandya**, effectively shutting down that particular negotiating track — at least for now. The deal had stalled over MI's insistence on receiving **both Shivam Dube and Ayush Mhatre** in any swap, a package CSK were not willing to offer given how highly they rate Mhatre. Mumbai's official spokesperson has publicly **denied** that Pandya is being actively shopped to any franchise, pushing back on the wave of trade reports that had built up over recent days. That denial sits alongside continuing reports of separate interest from **Delhi Capitals, Kolkata Knight Riders and Rajasthan Royals**, none of which have been confirmed. As of now, **no trade involving Pandya has been finalized**, and his status for the coming IPL season remains an open question.
stories.why_it_matters: Hardik Pandya is one of the IPL's most valuable and marketable all-rounders, and his franchise future affects team-building strategy, ticket sales and broadcast interest well beyond just Mumbai Indians and CSK — this kind of high-profile trade saga is a genuine off-season storyline that shapes fan expectations for the next season.
stories.ripple_effects: Other franchises reportedly interested (Delhi, Kolkata, Rajasthan) may now step up their own approaches to MI now that the CSK track has cooled, and Mumbai Indians' public denial adds uncertainty about whether Pandya stays captain or moves at all before the next auction cycle.
stories.why_now: The story is a direct continuation of an escalating trade saga that's been building over recent days, with MI's pullback from CSK talks marking the first concrete setback in the negotiations.
stories.watch_next: Whether any of the other reportedly interested franchises — Delhi Capitals, KKR or Rajasthan Royals — step forward with a formal offer now that the CSK track has stalled.
stories.the_lesson: In any negotiation, a deal collapses when one side's minimum ask exceeds what the other side is willing to give up — here, MI's insistence on a rising young talent (Mhatre), not just an established player, was the sticking point.

stories.title: Guyana Amazon Warriors beat San Francisco Unicorns by 6 runs to defend their Global Super League title
key_points: **Guyana Amazon Warriors** successfully defended their title, beating **San Francisco Unicorns by 6 runs** in the 2026 Global Super League final at Providence Stadium.
Guyana posted **85 runs**; the Unicorns fell just short at **79**, with the match decided inside **18.3 overs**.
All-rounder **Dwaine Pretorius** was Player of the Match, finishing unbeaten on **17 and taking 3 wickets for 24 runs**.
**Mohammad Nabi** of Guyana was named Player of the Series, having scored **53 runs and taken 10 wickets** across the tournament.
For the Unicorns — fresh off winning **Major League Cricket 2026** in the US — it was a first-ever GSL final appearance, ending in heartbreak.
stories.background: The **Global Super League (GSL)** is a T10-style franchise tournament based in Guyana, drawing teams and players from across the global T20 circuit, including US-based franchises expanding the sport's footprint in North America. San Francisco Unicorns arrived at this final on a hot streak, having just won **Major League Cricket 2026** in the United States and then beating Desert Vipers by 8 wickets in Friday's qualifier to reach their first-ever GSL final. Guyana Amazon Warriors, by contrast, were the tournament's most consistent side all season — finishing top of the league table and entering the final as defending champions with home advantage at Providence Stadium.
stories.what_happened: **Guyana Amazon Warriors** successfully defended their **Global Super League** title, beating the **San Francisco Unicorns by 6 runs** in Saturday's final at **Providence Stadium** in Guyana. Batting first, Guyana were bowled out for **85**, a modest total built around a late unbeaten **17 from Dwaine Pretorius**. In reply, the Unicorns fell short at **79**, with the match wrapped up inside **18.3 overs** in a low-scoring, tightly contested finish. **Pretorius** was named **Player of the Match** for his all-round contribution — 17 not out with the bat and **3 wickets for 24 runs** with the ball. Teammate **Mohammad Nabi** was named **Player of the Series**, having contributed **53 runs and 10 wickets** across the tournament. For the Unicorns, it capped a remarkable run that included a **Major League Cricket 2026** title and a comprehensive **8-wicket win over Desert Vipers** in the qualifier — but their first-ever GSL final appearance ended in a narrow defeat.
stories.why_it_matters: It caps a breakout year for US-based T20 cricket, with a genuinely competitive American franchise reaching a major international final, even in defeat — a sign the sport's US expansion is producing real on-field quality, not just novelty.
stories.ripple_effects: Expect Guyana Amazon Warriors' back-to-back title defense to boost the profile of Caribbean domestic T20 cricket, while the Unicorns' run adds momentum to the broader push to grow the sport's US fanbase and talent pool ahead of future US-hosted global events.
stories.why_now: The final was always scheduled for this date; the result closes out this year's Global Super League tournament.
stories.watch_next: Whether any Unicorns players parlay this run into selection for bigger T20 franchise leagues elsewhere, given the tournament's showcase value.
stories.the_lesson: A low-scoring final, decided by just 6 runs, is a reminder that in short-format cricket even a modest total can be defended with disciplined bowling — chasing isn't automatically the safer option.

stories.title: Table-topping Jaffna Kings, already through to the playoffs, face bottom-placed Dambulla Sixers today as the Lanka Premier League's group stage wraps up
key_points: **Jaffna Kings** sit top of the 2026 Lanka Premier League table with **5 wins from 7 games (10 points)** and have already secured a **playoff spot**.
**Dambulla Sixers** are bottom of the table, having won just once in six games, and must beat Jaffna today and hope other results fall their way to have any hope of survival.

Bangladesh batter **Towhid Hridoy**, brought in only after teammate Taskin Ahmed withdrew, has hit **35 off 21 and 31 off 8** in his first two Jaffna innings — form that helped drag the team off the bottom of the table.
Multiple franchises made **late squad changes** this week: Dambulla added Zimbabwe's **Sikandar Raza**, while Galle Gallants lost **Chris Lynn** (injury) and **Mehidy Hasan Miraz** (early departure).
The **LPL playoffs** begin August 5 at the R. Premadasa Stadium in Colombo, with the final set for August 8.
stories.background: The **Lanka Premier League (LPL)** is Sri Lanka Cricket's flagship T20 franchise tournament, a shop window that mixes international stars with young Sri Lankan talent and returned this year after a two-year hiatus, with the 2026 season opening on July 17. Six franchises play a round-robin, and the **top four** advance to a knockout stage. Because overseas players in T20 leagues are often on short-term deals tied to their national team's schedule, squads change constantly mid-tournament — as seen this week with several franchises swapping players in and out just before the final round-robin fixtures. Today's Dambulla vs Jaffna match at **Pallekele International Cricket Stadium** is effectively the last item of unfinished business before the playoff picture is set.
stories.what_happened: Jaffna Kings have been the form team of the tournament, winning five of seven games to top the table and already banking a playoff berth, with **Towhid Hridoy** — signed only as a late replacement — playing a key role in two rapid cameos since joining. Dambulla Sixers, by contrast, have won just once in six games and sit at the bottom, having lost their last three matches in a row, including a defeat to Colombo Kaps earlier this week. Ahead of today's meeting, Dambulla brought in Zimbabwe all-rounder **Sikandar Raza** as an injury replacement, while other franchises reshuffled too: Galle Gallants (currently top of the table on the back of a strong campaign) lost Australian batter Chris Lynn to injury and let Mehidy Hasan Miraz depart early, bringing in Australia's Thomas Rogers as cover. With the playoffs — an Eliminator and Qualifier 1 on August 5, Qualifier 2 on August 7 and the final on August 8, all at the Premadasa Stadium in Colombo — now just days away, today's result and net run rate could still shape who finishes where.
stories.why_it_matters: For Jaffna, the match is about seeding and momentum heading into a playoff run; for Dambulla, it is close to a must-win-and-hope scenario just to keep their season alive, and likely their last real chance to salvage pride either way. The pattern of last-minute squad reshuffles across nearly every franchise also shows how heavily modern T20 leagues depend on international players' short, overlapping windows of availability.
stories.ripple_effects: A big Jaffna win, or a big margin of victory generally, can shift net run rate calculations that decide which of Colombo Kaps, Kandy Royals and Galle Gallants join Jaffna in the top four. Players like Hridoy and Voll-type late replacements who perform well in these final matches also raise their stock for the next franchise-league auction cycle.
stories.why_now: This is the last round-robin fixture of the 2026 season before the top four are locked in and the knockouts begin on August 5, so it is the final chance for placement in the table to change.
stories.watch_next: The final league-stage results today to confirm which four teams join Jaffna Kings in the playoffs, followed by the Eliminator and Qualifier 1 on August 5 at the Premadasa Stadium.

key_terms.definition: A tie-breaker used in T20 tournaments that measures how much faster a team scores its runs compared to how fast it concedes them across the tournament; it decides final league-table positions when teams are level on points.
Playoff-stage matches in T20 tournaments: the Eliminator is a knockout game between the 3rd and 4th-placed teams, while Qualifier 1 lets the top two teams fight for a direct spot in the final.

stories.the_lesson: In short, congested T20 leagues, squads are never fixed — international call-ups and injuries mean a late replacement player can end up deciding who makes the playoffs, so form in the tournament's final week often matters more than how a team started it.

stories.title: Ellyse Perry's unbeaten 68 drags Birmingham Phoenix Women to their first win of the season, beating Welsh Fire with a ball to spare
key_points: Birmingham Phoenix Women chased down Welsh Fire's 144/3 to win by **7 wickets**, getting there with just **one ball to spare**.
Australian veteran **Ellyse Perry** anchored the chase, finishing unbeaten on **68 off 46 balls** and was named Player of the Match.
Perry and **Alice Capsey** (51 off 29) put on an **86-run stand** that turned a stuttering chase into a win.
Welsh Fire's total was built around a blazing **78 from 22-year-old Georgia Voll**, one of Australia's fastest-rising batters.
The win is Phoenix's **first of the 2026 Hundred season**, ending a winless start to their campaign.
stories.background: **The Hundred** is England and Wales' short-format franchise cricket competition, launched by the ECB in 2021 to bring new, younger and more casual fans to the sport. Each side faces **100 balls per innings** (instead of the 120 balls of a normal T20), split into blocks of five or ten, which speeds up the game and gives bowlers a slightly different tactical puzzle. Birmingham Phoenix Women had gone the opening weeks of this season without a win, while **Ellyse Perry** — regarded as one of the greatest all-rounders the women's game has produced, and Australia's youngest-ever senior international when she debuted in 2007 — was signed specifically to add experience and finishing power to their top order. Welsh Fire, meanwhile, had been leaning on Voll, a young Australian batter who broke into her national side only in the last year and has quickly become one of the most sought-after overseas signings in franchise cricket.
stories.what_happened: Playing at **Edgbaston** in Birmingham on August 1, Welsh Fire posted **144 for 3**, built on Georgia Voll's **78 off 55 balls**, who started slowly through the powerplay before accelerating hard against the spinners and bringing up her half-century with a six. Chasing 145, Birmingham Phoenix lost early momentum before **Perry and Alice Capsey** came together and added **86 runs for the third wicket**, with Capsey striking 51 off just 29 balls. Capsey had also taken two wickets earlier in the Welsh Fire innings, making it a strong all-round game for her. Perry finished the job herself, hitting Welsh Fire bowler Heather Graham for **10 runs in two balls** at the death to get Phoenix home with just one ball remaining, sealing a **seven-wicket win** and her side's first victory of the season.
stories.why_it_matters: For a Birmingham Phoenix side that had started the season without a win, this breaks the losing run and lifts them off the bottom of the table with group games running out before the playoffs. It is also a reminder that in a young, fast-scoring format, experienced campaigners like Perry can still decide games in the final overs.
stories.ripple_effects: The result nudges Welsh Fire down the table and tightens the run-in for the remaining top-four spots in The Hundred Women's Competition. It also raises Georgia Voll's profile further — another big score adds to a breakout season that is likely to increase her value to franchise-league recruiters worldwide, including at the IPL-linked WPL and Australia's WBBL.
stories.why_now: The Hundred's group stage is entering its final fortnight, so every result now carries real weight for who reaches the knockouts, which is why a routine-looking group match is generating this much attention.
stories.watch_next: Whether Birmingham Phoenix can string together back-to-back wins in their remaining group games to force their way into playoff contention.

key_terms.definition: An England and Wales franchise cricket competition where each team faces 100 balls per innings instead of the usual 120-ball T20 over, designed to be a shorter, simpler entry point for new fans.
A player skilled enough at both batting and bowling to be picked for either discipline, making them especially valuable in short-format cricket.

stories.the_lesson: In fast, chaotic short-format cricket, a single experienced partnership in the middle overs can out-value a flashy start — composure under pressure at the death often matters more than raw firepower earlier in an innings.

stories.title: Bangladesh get a big boost as wicketkeeper Litton Das returns to the squad for their historic Australia Test tour
key_points: **Litton Das**, Bangladesh's experienced wicketkeeper-batter, has been **added back** to the squad for the first Test against Australia.
He'd been out with a **calf injury** sustained during the third ODI against Australia at home on **June 14**.
The Bangladesh Cricket Board confirmed his inclusion on **Saturday, August 1**, citing encouraging progress in rehab.
The first Test starts in **Darwin on August 13** — Bangladesh's **first-ever Test appearance in Australia**.
The squad remains **pace-depleted**: strike bowler **Nahid Rana** is out with a side strain, and **Shoriful Islam** misses out with a hamstring injury.
stories.background: Bangladesh named their squad for this historic two-Test tour of Australia (Darwin August 13–17, Mackay August 22–26) last week, but it was a squad short on fast-bowling firepower and, notably, without a single player who'd previously played a Test in Australian conditions — a tough ask against a team that dominates at home. Litton Das is one of Bangladesh's most experienced white-ball and red-ball wicketkeeper-batters, and his absence would have been a significant loss of both batting depth and glovework experience for a squad already facing a steep challenge.
stories.what_happened: The **Bangladesh Cricket Board** announced on **Saturday, August 1**, that **Litton Das** has been added to the squad for the opening Test against Australia in Darwin, after showing encouraging progress recovering from a **calf injury** he suffered during the third ODI against Australia at home on **June 14**. His return significantly strengthens a squad that had been announced as **pace-depleted** just days earlier — with lead strike bowler **Nahid Rana** ruled out by a side strain and left-arm seamer **Shoriful Islam** missing out through a hamstring injury, and uncapped fast bowler **Musfik Hasan** getting a first call-up as pace cover. Litton is scheduled to join the squad in Australia as preparations intensify for the **August 13** series opener in Darwin — a tour that marks Bangladesh's first-ever Test appearances on Australian soil.
stories.why_it_matters: Litton's return restores badly needed batting and wicketkeeping experience to a touring squad that otherwise has zero players with prior Test experience in Australian conditions — a meaningful boost for a team already facing a historically dominant home side.
stories.ripple_effects: It likely settles Bangladesh's wicketkeeper question for the series and adds middle-order batting stability, partially offsetting the pace-bowling concerns that defined the squad announcement just days ago.
stories.why_now: The BCB's confirmation came Saturday, days before the squad is due to assemble in Australia ahead of the August 13 series opener.
stories.watch_next: Litton's first appearance in the nets in Australia, and whether he's fully match-fit for the Darwin Test opener.
stories.the_lesson: A squad announcement is rarely the final word — injury recoveries and late call-ups can meaningfully reshape a touring party's balance in the days before a series actually begins.

stories.title: Babar Azam — not Shan Masood — leads Pakistan into today's must-win second Test as Shafique and Shakeel fight for a spot
key_points: Pakistan's likely XI for the second Test has **Babar Azam as captain**, with **Mohammad Rizwan** keeping wicket.
Head coach **Sarfaraz Ahmed** said the final call between **Abdullah Shafique** and **Saud Shakeel** — both filling in for the injured Shan Masood — won't be made until the **toss**.
Uncapped batter **Awais Zafar** remains a **third option** for Masood's middle-order spot.
Masood's finger fracture was **confirmed by PCB on Thursday** after a scan and clinical assessment.
Pakistan trail the series **1-0** and must win at Queen's Park Oval just to draw it.
stories.background: Pakistan lost the first Test of this two-match series by 90 runs at Tarouba despite a Shan Masood century, collapsing to 120 all out while chasing 211. Masood was hit on the finger by West Indies quick Jayden Seales during that innings and has since been ruled out of the second Test. Abdullah Shafique and Saud Shakeel were added to the squad earlier in the tour after another batter, Abdullah Fazal, was ruled out with a back injury — meaning Pakistan already had cover in place before Masood's injury.
stories.what_happened: As the second Test began today, **August 2**, at Queen's Park Oval in Port of Spain, Pakistan's likely playing XI confirmed **Babar Azam as captain**, with **Mohammad Rizwan** behind the stumps. Head coach **Sarfaraz Ahmed** said the choice between **Abdullah Shafique** and **Saud Shakeel** to fill Masood's middle-order spot would only be finalized at the **toss**, with uncapped batter **Awais Zafar** still technically in contention as a third option. Masood's **fractured left index finger** — sustained batting through pain during Pakistan's first-Test century — was formally confirmed by the **Pakistan Cricket Board** on Thursday following a scan and clinical assessment, and rules him out of this match entirely. Pakistan enter the Test trailing the series **1-0** after their 90-run defeat in Tarouba, meaning only a win keeps the series alive.
stories.why_it_matters: A series-defining Test is already high stakes; going in with an unsettled batting XI and no clarity until the toss adds real uncertainty for a team that can't afford another batting collapse like the 120 all out that cost them the first Test.
stories.ripple_effects: A poor result here would hand West Indies a rare series sweep over Pakistan and add pressure on Pakistan's team management heading into their next assignment, a three-Test series in England starting August 19 — a tour Masood's own participation in remains uncertain given his injury.
stories.why_now: The match started today, and the final XI decision is being made at the toss.
stories.watch_next: The toss result and confirmed XI, and how Pakistan's batting responds after last Test's collapse.
stories.the_lesson: In Test cricket, a team's depth is really tested not by its first-choice XI but by how well its bench performs when injuries force changes — Pakistan's next few days hinge on options they hoped not to need.
